01The bat

The bat takes the long way to the ball

This is the one to work on. It is also the one that would add the most bat speed.

Bat to your front arm37°should be near zero
Back arm at the finish162°18° from straight
Bat speed79.7 mphyour real number
Swing to swing±3.4 mphbarely moves

Stand the bat straight up in your stance. It should line up with your front arm, like two train tracks. Yours sits 37° away from it.

That sounds small. It is not. It means the bat starts its trip to the ball from above your hands instead of from behind them, and a bat coming from above has further to travel and less room to be wrong.

We can see the same thing later in the swing too. As the bat comes through, your back arm should be reaching out almost straight. Yours stops 18 degrees short. Two different moments, same story.

Here is the part that should make you feel good about it: you do this the same way every single time. Your bat speed is 79.7 mph and it moves by less than 3.4 mph from swing to swing. A repeatable swing with one thing wrong is much easier to fix than a swing that does something different every rep.

The green stripe is where a good swing sits. The dot is you. The little bar through the dot is how much you change from swing to swing — yours are short, which means these are real, not one bad rep.

Work on this

The short versionThe bat comes down from above. Get it behind your hands instead.

02The load

You fixed most of this yourself

The load is everything before your front foot lands. Nobody coached this and it got better anyway in five days.

Back hip over back foot0.2 inoutside — basically stacked
Slide toward the catcher0.9 indown from last week
Head behind your belt2.0 inshould be in front
Front foot to the ball173 mssame every time

Last week your back hip sat 1.5 in to the inside of your back foot. Now it is stacked on it, within 0.2 in. Last week you slid 2.1 in back toward the catcher as you loaded. Now it is 0.9 in. Your hips also stay flatter at the top of your leg lift than they did.

One thing did not come along: your head. When your front foot lands, your head is still 2.0 inches behind your belt buckle. It should be in front of it. Your body moved forward and your head stayed put.

That is a much smaller fix than it sounds, and it is in the plan below.

Three of these four are in or near the green now. The bottom one is the head.

03Landing and contact

You land in a good spot, on time, every time

From front foot down to hitting the ball takes you 173 ms. That is about a fifth of a second, and it is the same on every swing.

Where your hips land49 %right in the middle
Hips toward the plate1.0 inwrong way
Arrowhead extension193 in²the space between your arms and your body
Bat holds its line22 msafter you hit it

When your front foot lands, your hips are sitting 49 % of the way between your feet — right in the middle, which is where they should be. Your hips are level. This is a good landing and there is nothing to change about it.

The one thing worth knowing: after you land, your hips slide about 1.0 inches toward the plate. They should be going the other way, clearing space for your hands. Moving toward the plate crowds the exact space your bat needs — which is another version of the problem in section 01. Fix the bat path and this usually comes with it.

The bottom two have no green stripe because there is no agreed “good” number for them yet. They are here so we can see if they change next time.

Good

The short versionGreat landing. Your hips just drift the wrong way afterwards.

04One to ignore

You may have been told your hips fire in the wrong order

They do. We are telling you not to work on it, and you deserve to know why.

In a swing, your hips are supposed to turn fastest first, then your chest, then your arms, then the bat. Yours goes chest first. It does it on every swing of both days, so the measurement is not a fluke.

The first version of this report made that your number one thing to fix. That was a mistake and we are correcting it. When we went back and checked it against the research, two things came up. Turning in the “wrong” order shows up in about half of the best hitters ever measured. And how far your hips turn ahead of your shoulders barely relates to bat speed at all.

So it stays on the list as something we measure and watch. It is not something to build your practice around. The bat path is, and it is not close.

Watch, do not train

The short versionReal, measured, and not your problem right now.

What to do

Three things, in this order. The third one is “leave it alone”, and it counts.

  1. Get the bat behind your hands, not on top of them.

    Hold the bat straight up. It should line up with your front arm. Yours is 37° away from it, and that is the biggest single thing we measured. It means the bat starts its trip to the ball from above instead of from behind. Hit off a high tee — if the bat comes over the top you will miss under the ball and you will know straight away. One-handed front-arm swings do the same job.

    What good looks like: the bat and your front arm look like train tracks.

  2. Get your head in front of your belt buckle when you land.

    Right now it is 2.0 inches behind it. Here is the good news: your body already fixed the hard half of this by itself in five days. Your back hip sits over your back foot now and you barely slide backwards any more. It is just your head that stayed behind. Pick something to look at out in front and keep your eyes going to it.

    What good looks like: your head gets to your belt buckle by the time your front foot lands.

  3. Do not change anything else.

    You swing at 79.7 mph and it hardly moves from swing to swing. That is a good thing and it is worth protecting. You may have been told your hips and shoulders fire in the wrong order. They do — but we checked, and it turns out that matters a lot less than people think, and about half of the best hitters ever measured do the same thing. Leave it alone. Work on the bat and the head, and we measure again.

    What good looks like: bat speed goes up and stays just as steady.
